source.title: Finding Features in Neural Networks with the Empirical NTK

record.tranche_reason: The post measures empirical-NTK eigenspectra and eigenvector alignment with known features in toy models, including Toy Models of Superposition. This is a different measurement from directly measuring the models’ feature-storage geometry.
record.gate_note: The post reports its own eNTK results on Toy Models of Superposition and modular-arithmetic models. It does not report LLM experiments; the Malladi et al. result is cited background and is not recorded as a result from this study. Specific TMS sweep settings and numerical cosine similarities are not given in the post text.
record.test_reason: The post uses Toy Models of Superposition and a modular-arithmetic MLP as benchmarks with known ground-truth features. It reports how well its own method works: eNTK spectrum cliffs and eigenvector alignment with those features. It does not measure the superposition geometry itself (overlap, near-orthogonality, a sparsity-dependent transition) or polysemanticity. It runs no LLM or SAE experiments. Its results show whether the eNTK finds features, not whether any claim version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The author concludes that eNTK eigenstructure aligns with ground-truth features in the toy models studied and can track grokking. The author calls this a preliminary sign for feature discovery, with Transformer experiments left as future work.
record.recipe_differences: The post measures eNTK spectra and eigenvector-to-feature alignment, rather than directly measuring the feature-storage geometry studied in Toy Models of Superposition. It also applies this analysis to a modular-arithmetic MLP.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported TMS analysis varies hidden-layer size and sparsity; the post notes an importance-rescaling sweep over β in the paper and shows β=0.3. In modular arithmetic, the reported spectrum changes over training, with the second cliff appearing around grokking.

fits_no_version.finding: In Toy Models of Superposition (n=50, I=0.8), the flattened eNTK spectrum has two cliffs. They track the number of features the model reconstructs and the total number of features. After importance rescaling, the top eigenvectors align with ground-truth features in both the sparse and dense regimes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: eNTK eigenspaces recover ground-truth features in toy superposition models.

fits_no_version.finding: In a modular-arithmetic MLP, the eNTK eigenspaces align with Fourier feature families, and a second cliff appears around grokking.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In modular-arithmetic MLPs, eNTK eigenspaces track Fourier feature structure and the grokking transition.

record.problems: The post gives no numerical cosine similarities or specific values for the TMS m and S sweep in its text. It reports qualitative alignment and spectrum descriptions, without uncertainty estimates or controls. The post says Transformer evaluation is future work.
record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2 'tests V1' guess was overturned. The TMS model is used only as a benchmark with known features, so the post evaluates the eNTK method rather than superposition itself. The Malladi et al. result is cited background.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not directly measure feature overlap, pairwise orthogonality, the model’s stored feature directions, or a sparsity-dependent transition in the storage geometry. It reports eNTK eigenspectrum cliffs and eNTK-eigenvector alignment with ground-truth feature vectors.
The post does not test whether capacity competition explains polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The post does not investigate polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity.
No LLM experiments are reported. The post discusses Transformer experiments as future work and cites a separate study on eNTK fine-tuning performance.
The post does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
The post reports alignment of eNTK eigenvectors with feature vectors, but does not test whether the features superposed in a network are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.
